## About the workshop

Open and reproducible science helps others understand, evaluate, reuse,
and extend research. In this 90-minute workshop, we follow one prepared
R project from its source data to an archived result. We use
`HealthWellbeing` to pool published correlations between health and
well-being.
[Teaching dataset](workshop/00_preparation.qmd#preparation-data)

The workshop is presented by [James Bristow](2_coordinators.qmd#james-bristow), Massey University, with co-author [Hana Liang](2_coordinators.qmd#hana-liang), Bioeconomy Science Institute.

The main aim is for you to understand and experience an end-to-end
reproducible research workflow, not to master every individual package.

## Learning objectives

By the end of the workshop, participants should be able to:

-   Explain how the tools support different parts of a reproducible research workflow.
-   Describe how a codebook and structured metadata record variables,
    provenance, licensing, and access conditions in support of FAIR principles.
-   Explain how `pins` and `vetiver` link results to specific data and model versions.
-   Complete and run a `targets` pipeline and render a Quarto report from its outputs.
-   Modify an analysis input, rebuild only what is affected, and reproduce the result.
-   Identify the files and metadata needed for a citable release and archive.

The session combines 42 minutes of concepts and demonstrations, 40
minutes of hands-on exercises, and 8 minutes of discussion.

## One dataset, one exercise, one environment

-   **One dataset throughout.** Every stage uses `HealthWellbeing`. For
    `vetiver`, a small supplementary predictive model stands in for the
    meta-analysis model, which its standard interface does not support.
-   **One continuous hands-on exercise.** You complete and run a
    partially completed `targets` pipeline and Quarto report, then
    change the analysis and reproduce the results, rather than building
    everything from scratch.
-   **One prepared computational environment.** MyBinder provides the
    packages, configuration, and data, so nothing is installed during
    the workshop. [Preparation](workshop/00_preparation.qmd)

## Supplementary exercise

Synthetic data with `synthpop` is a supplementary exercise for after
the workshop. The archiving segment mentions it briefly when
discussing data that cannot be shared.
[Synthetic data with synthpop](workshop/10_synthetic_data.qmd)

## Reproducibility when data cannot be shared

Open science can include restricted-access data. Researchers can document their methods, code, and access conditions while restricting the original observations.

Synthetic data can help readers test whether a workflow runs. Verifying
findings based on original observations requires access to those
observations. A differential privacy claim requires a validated
mechanism and privacy accounting [@near2021-synthetic-data].

## Principles to put into practice {#intro-principles}

Throughout the session, consider whether another researcher could:

-   **Understand** the purpose of the project and follow the analysis decisions.
-   **Reproduce** the environment and rerun the workflow on another machine.
-   **Audit** the history of changes and the relationship between inputs and outputs.
-   **Trace** a reported result to the versions of its data, fitted model, and software environment.
-   **Reuse and extend** the code and materials with clear documentation and licensing.
-   **Assess sharing limits** and distinguish a runnable workflow from verification of restricted-data findings.
-   **Find and cite** a preserved version of the research outputs.

We will consider common barriers to these goals, including undocumented dependencies, manual analysis steps, and assumptions tied to a single computing environment.

## Getting started

Some familiarity with R will help you follow the examples. Open the
prepared environment, verify the teaching dataset, and prepare the
dataset versions before the timed session.
